chapter_title: Memory and I/O: Screen and Keyboard
chapter_summary:
Input and output (I/O) are how the computer communicates with the outside world. The Hack computer uses a simple but powerful technique called **memory-mapped I/O**, where I/O devices are treated as memory locations. Writing to certain memory addresses updates the screen, and reading from a certain address returns the state of the keyboard.

**Memory-mapped I/O:**

In memory-mapped I/O, there is no separate I/O bus or I/O instructions. Instead, I/O devices are assigned addresses in the memory space. The CPU reads and writes to these addresses just like any other memory location, but the hardware intercepts these accesses and performs the appropriate I/O operation.

Advantages of memory-mapped I/O:
- **Simplicity:** No special I/O instructions are needed. The same load and store instructions work for both memory and I/O.
- **Uniformity:** I/O devices can be accessed using the same addressing modes as memory.
- **Flexibility:** New I/O devices can be added by assigning them memory addresses.

**The Hack screen:**

The Hack screen is a black-and-white display with 256 rows and 512 columns of pixels. Each pixel is either black (1) or white (0). The screen is memory-mapped to addresses 16384 to 24575 (8K words). Each word controls 16 pixels (one row of 16 pixels). The screen is organized as 256 rows, with 32 words per row (32 × 16 = 512 pixels per row).

To draw a pixel at row r, column c:
1. Compute the word address: `Screen[r * 32 + c / 16]`
2. Compute the bit position within the word: `c % 16`
3. Set the corresponding bit to 1 (black) or 0 (white).

For example, to draw a black pixel at row 0, column 0:
- Address = 16384 + 0 * 32 + 0 / 16 = 16384
- Bit position = 0 % 16 = 0
- Write `1` to bit 0 of address 16384.

To draw a black pixel at row 0, column 17:
- Address = 16384 + 0 * 32 + 17 / 16 = 16384 + 1 = 16385
- Bit position = 17 % 16 = 1
- Write `1` to bit 1 of address 16385.

**The Hack keyboard:**

The keyboard is memory-mapped to address 24576. Reading from this address returns the ASCII code of the currently pressed key. If no key is pressed, the value is 0. The keyboard interface is extremely simple: it is a read-only register that the hardware updates whenever a key is pressed or released.

**Keyboard codes:**
- The keyboard returns ASCII codes for printable characters (e.g., 'A' = 65, '0' = 48).
- Special keys have extended codes: newline = 128, backspace = 129, left arrow = 130, up arrow = 131, right arrow = 132, down arrow = 133, home = 134, end = 135, page up = 136, page down = 137, insert = 138, delete = 139, escape = 140, F1-F12 = 141-152.

**Building the complete computer:**

The complete Hack computer is built from three chips:
1. **CPU:** The processor we built in the previous chapter.
2. **Memory:** The RAM16K chip we built, plus the screen and keyboard memory maps. The Memory chip combines data memory, screen, and keyboard into a single addressable space.
3. **ROM:** The instruction memory. This is provided by the simulator and loads the program from a file.

The Computer chip connects these three components:
```hdl
CHIP Computer {
    IN reset;

    PARTS:
    ROM32K(address=pc, out=instruction);
    CPU(inM=inM, instruction=instruction, reset=reset, outM=outM, writeM=writeM, addressM=addressM, pc=pc);
    Memory(in=outM, load=writeM, address=addressM, out=inM);
}
```

The connections are:
- The PC output from the CPU is connected to the ROM address input (fetching the next instruction).
- The ROM output (instruction) is connected to the CPU instruction input.
- The CPU's outM, writeM, and addressM are connected to the Memory chip (writing to data memory or screen).
- The Memory output (inM) is connected to the CPU's inM input (reading from data memory or keyboard).
- The reset signal initializes the computer (resets the PC to 0).

This is the complete computer! It fetches instructions from ROM, executes them in the CPU, and reads/writes data from/to memory. The screen and keyboard are part of the memory space, so programs can draw graphics and read keyboard input simply by writing to and reading from memory addresses.

screens.title: Memory and I/O: Screen and Keyboard
screens.subtitle: How the Hack computer maps graphics and keyboard input into RAM

narration.text: In this chapter we explore the Hack computer's approach to input and output, which uses memory-mapped input and output to treat devices like ordinary memory locations. You will learn how a 256 by 512 black-and-white screen is represented as 8K words in R A M, how each 16-bit word controls 16 horizontal pixels, and how a single read-only memory address reports the currently pressed key. Understanding this mapping teaches you how software and hardware meet: software computes addresses and bit positions, and hardware interprets reads and writes as display or keyboard actions. We'll ground this with concrete examples — calculating the word and bit for given row and column values, and a short program outline that fills the middle row with black pixels. Finally, you'll see how the Computer chip wires the C P U, Memory, and ROM together so programs can fetch instructions, compute addresses, and write to the screen. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain why memory-mapped input and output is simple and flexible, and you'll be ready to write small programs that draw pixels and read keyboard codes.

keyIdea.title: Memory-mapped I/O unifies devices and memory
keyIdea.text: Treating screen and keyboard as mapped memory addresses lets the CPU use standard load/store instructions to draw pixels and read keys, simplifying hardware and software.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Memory & I/O
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Memory and I/O: Screen and Keyboard

Explore how the Hack computer maps a 256×512 monochrome screen and a keyboard into RAM, and how the complete Computer chip lets programs draw and read input using ordinary memory operations.

In this lesson
Understand memory-mapped I/O, compute screen addresses and bits, read keyboard codes, and assemble the CPU+Memory+ROM wiring.
Why it matters
You will directly control pixels and sense key presses using the same instructions used for RAM. This reduces hardware complexity.
Coming up
Examples: pixel address math, a program to draw a middle line, and reading the keyboard register.
Explore Key Topics
Screen Map
16384–24575: 8K words, each word controls 16 pixels.
Keyboard
Address 24576. Reads return ASCII or 0 if no key.
Computer Chip
CPU + Memory + ROM wired so programs can fetch and read/write memory-mapped devices.
Visual Concept
Memory City: Screen billboard and Keyboard sensor
Imagine the 16K memory as a city. The screen district occupies a continuous block of addresses; each word is a short billboard controlling 16 lights. The keyboard is a single sensor reporting the last pressed key. Programs are painters and couriers that write to these addresses.
Key Takeaway
Memory-mapped I/O lets the CPU use ordinary memory instructions to update the screen and read keyboard input, keeping the hardware simple and the programming model uniform.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will understand the memory-mapped input and output model and how the Hack computer maps its screen and keyboard into the R A M address space. You will be able to compute the exact memory address and bit position needed to change a single pixel, and you will implement the keyboard as a single read-only register. You will also assemble the complete Computer chip by wiring the C P U, Memory, and ROM so a program can fetch instructions and read or write input and output using normal memory operations. Each objective trains a practical skill: calculating addresses for graphics, performing read-modify-write updates to set or clear pixels, and writing small programs to draw a horizontal line or to wait for and display a key press. These abilities matter because they reveal how low-level software manipulates hardware state and why the Hack design chooses simplicity and uniformity over special input and output instructions. Finally, you'll be prepared to test these behaviors in the simulator and reason about trade-offs such as code complexity versus hardware simplicity.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Practice Goals
Hands-on Tasks
  • Compute base address for row 128: add 16384 + 128*32, then write 0xFFFF to 32 consecutive words to make a black horizontal line.
  • Poll the keyboard register at address 24576; when non-zero, display the ASCII code on the screen.

Quick example
To set the first pixel at row 0, col 0: address = 16384; bit = 0; write a word with bit 0 set. To set col 17: address = 16384 + 1; bit = 1.
Why these tasks?
They combine address arithmetic, bit masking, and simple control flow — core skills for low-level programming and hardware understanding.

screens.title: Memory-mapped I/O explained
screens.subtitle: I/O devices appear as memory addresses; the CPU uses regular load/store operations

narration.text: Memory-mapped input and output means the C P U reads and writes device registers using the same instructions it uses for ordinary R A M. There is no separate input and output bus or special input and output instructions. The hardware assigns ranges of memory addresses to devices — for the Hack computer the screen occupies addresses 16384 through 24575 and the keyboard sits at 24576 — and intercepts accesses to those ranges. Practically, this simplifies the C P U: you reuse fetch, load, and store logic instead of adding special support for input and output. A concrete example is writing M = D to a screen word. The same assembler instruction that writes a variable in R A M will light 16 pixels when executed at a screen address. A common misconception is that memory-mapped input and output hides device complexity; it does not. The programmer must still compute addresses and bit positions for pixels, and must often perform read-modify-write sequences to change single pixels inside a 16-bit word. The payoff is uniformity: addressing modes and instructions work the same for device registers and data memory. Consider how adding a new device becomes a matter of reserving addresses instead of inventing new C P U opcodes.

keyIdea.title: Uniform access pattern
keyIdea.text: Memory-mapped I/O uses the same memory instructions for devices and RAM, keeping the CPU design simple while requiring address and bit math at the software level.

content.html:
Module 3 › Memory-mapped I/O › Definition
Definition

I/O as memory locations

The CPU accesses devices by reading and writing addresses in the same memory space. No special opcodes are required.

Advantages
  • Simple CPU design: reuse load/store logic.
  • Uniform addressing: same modes for memory and devices.
  • Flexible expansion: add devices by reserving addresses.
Key Takeaway

Memory-mapped I/O trades a bit of programmer arithmetic for much simpler hardware; devices behave like memory words.

Concrete example and misconception
Example:
Writing M = D to address 16384 sets 16 pixels controlled by that word. The same instruction that writes a variable in RAM now updates the screen.
Misconception:
Memory-mapped I/O does not remove the need for address math. You still compute which word and which bit represent a single pixel; the difference is the access mechanism.
Why this matters:
Uniformity reduces CPU complexity and makes device access part of the normal programming model, enabling flexible device additions and straightforward simulation.

screens.title: How the Hack screen maps pixels to words
screens.subtitle: 256 rows × 512 columns; 1 bit per pixel, 16 pixels per word

narration.text: The Hack screen is a monochrome bitmap with 256 rows and 512 columns, so it controls 256 × 512 = 131,072 pixels. Each pixel is one bit: 1 for black, 0 for white. Hardware maps this picture to memory addresses 16384 through 24575 — a contiguous block of 8,192 words. Each 16-bit word controls 16 horizontal pixels, and each screen row consists of 32 words, because 32 × 16 equals the 512 columns. To draw or clear one pixel the software computes the word index using row * 32 + column / 16, then the bit position within that word is column % 16. For example, row 0 column 0 maps to address 16384 and bit 0. Row 0 column 17 maps to address 16385 and bit 1. A common oversight is forgetting integer division versus remainder when computing the word and bit. Another implementation detail is that changing a single pixel often requires reading the current word, modifying the single bit, and writing the word back, otherwise you risk flipping neighboring pixels. Practice these steps to make pixel manipulation reliable.

keyIdea.title: 1 word -> 16 pixels
keyIdea.text: Each 16-bit memory word controls 16 horizontal pixels; rows contain 32 words and the screen occupies 8K words.

content.html:
Module 3 › Screen Map › Process
Specs

256 × 512 pixels

Total pixels: 131,072. Memory words: 8,192. Relationship: 1 word controls 16 pixels, so each row uses 32 words.

Address range
16384 — 24575 (inclusive) — exactly 8,192 words reserved for the screen.
Step-by-step: compute pixel word and bit
Step 1 — Word address
wordIndex = row * 32 + (column / 16)
Step 2 — Bit position
bit = column % 16
Final address
address = 16384 + wordIndex
Example
Row 0, Col 17 → wordIndex = 0*32 + 1 = 1 → address = 16385. Bit = 1. Writing bit 1 to that word sets the pixel at column 17.
Common Mistake
Using column/16 without integer division or using 16-bit index offsets incorrectly will place pixels in the wrong word.

screens.title: Address math and example writes
screens.subtitle: Formulas and concrete word/bit examples you can test

narration.text: Let's walk through the formulas and concrete examples you will use in code. The core formulas are: wordIndex = row * 32 + (column / 16), bit = column % 16, address = 16384 + wordIndex. These are integer operations: the division yields which 16-pixel word contains the column. Two short examples make this concrete. Example one: row 0, column 0 gives wordIndex 0 and bit 0, so address 16384 and set bit 0. Example two: row 0, column 17 gives wordIndex 1 and bit 1, so address 16385 and set bit 1. In practice, to set a single pixel you often perform a read-modify-write: read the 16-bit word at that address, set or clear the single bit, then write the word back. The read preserves the other 15 pixels handled by that word. A common trap for beginners is writing a mask without reading first, which erases neighbouring pixels. Below is a small illustrative snippet that shows the calculations and a conceptual loop that writes 0xFFFF across a row; run it in the simulator to confirm the results. Address math and example writes means work through specific row/column pairs and use read-modify-write to avoid clobbering neighbouring pixels.. In practical terms, formulas and concrete word/bit examples you can test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concrete examples prevent off-by-one errors
keyIdea.text: Work through specific row/column pairs and use read-modify-write to avoid clobbering neighbouring pixels.

content.html:
Module 3 › Address Math › Code Walkthrough
Formulas
// Compute the word and bit for a pixel
wordIndex = row * 32 + (column / 16)
bit      = column % 16
address  = 16384 + wordIndex

// Example: row 0, col 17
// wordIndex = 0*32 + 1 = 1
// bit = 1
// address = 16384 + 1 = 16385
Run these calculations with integer division for column/16 and use modulo for the bit.
Write pattern example
To draw an entire row with black pixels, set each of the 32 words in that row to 0xFFFF. Below is a conceptual loop you can implement in Hack assembly using the A register and M destination.
// Conceptual assembly outline
@SCREEN_BASE   // A = 16384 + row*32
D = -1         // D = 0xFFFF (all bits 1)
(LOOP)
@i
D; JGT?         // loop control omitted - conceptual
M = D           // write 0xFFFF to memory[address]
@ADDRESS+1
...              // increment address and repeat 32 times
Pro tip
Use a simple loop counter set to 32 to write exactly the words that form one row.

screens.title: The Hack keyboard register
screens.subtitle: A single read-only memory address returns ASCII or zero

narration.text: The keyboard is implemented as a single read-only register mapped to address 24576. Reading from that address returns the ASCII code for the currently pressed key, or zero if no key is pressed. Printable characters use their ASCII values — for example, 'A' equals 65 and '0' equals 48 — while special keys use higher numeric codes in a defined range: newline is 128, backspace 129, arrow keys 130–133, and function keys and other controls map to further codes. A key point to remember is that the register is updated by hardware as keys are pressed and released; your program simply repeatedly reads that address to detect state changes. A common mistake is assuming the keyboard produces a stream you must read sequentially. Instead, it is a snapshot register: each read returns the current code. If you need to detect a key press event, typical code polls the register until it becomes non-zero, captures that value, then optionally waits for it to return to zero to distinguish single presses. This simple interface keeps hardware minimal and lets software implement the desired behavior.

keyIdea.title: Keyboard is a read-only snapshot
keyIdea.text: Address 24576 returns the ASCII of the current key or 0 if none; software polls it to detect key presses.

content.html:
Module 3 › Keyboard › Definition
Keyboard register behavior
Address
24576 — read-only. Returns ASCII code of the currently pressed key or 0 if none.
Printable and special codes
Printable characters return standard ASCII values. Special keys occupy extended codes: newline 128, backspace 129, left arrow 130, up arrow 131, right arrow 132, down arrow 133, and further control codes up to function keys.
Common pattern
Poll address 24576 in a loop. When read value != 0, act on it. If you need a single-press detection, wait for the value to return to 0 before resuming detection.
Example
A program can repeatedly read the keyboard register; when the value is non-zero, it copies the ASCII code to a known screen location so the character becomes visible.
Misconception
Treating the keyboard as a FIFO stream is wrong. It is a live snapshot; your code must poll and implement buffering if desired.

screens.title: Draw a horizontal line in the middle row
screens.subtitle: Compute the base address for row 128 and write 0xFFFF to 32 words

narration.text: A practical exercise from the chapter is drawing a horizontal black line across the screen's middle row. The middle row index is 128. To find the row base address you compute 16384 + 128 * 32. That base points to the first of the 32 words for that row. Then you write 0xFFFF to each of those 32 addresses to turn every pixel in those words black. Conceptually you set a loop counter to 32, load the base address into A, and write the all-ones pattern to M while incrementing the address and decrementing the counter. An important subtlety is using the correct word-sized value 0xFFFF — since each word is 16 bits, 0xFFFF lights all 16 pixels controlled by that word. A common mistake is writing 1 instead of 0xFFFF: that sets only the least-significant bit across words. When you execute this program in the simulator you'll see a solid black stripe across row 128, confirming your address arithmetic and loop logic. Draw a horizontal line in the middle row means compute screen base for row 128 and write 0xffff to each of the 32 words in that row to draw a continuous black line.. In practical terms, compute the base address for row 128 and write 0xffff to 32 words. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Middle-row loop
keyIdea.text: Compute screen base for row 128 and write 0xFFFF to each of the 32 words in that row to draw a continuous black line.

content.html:
Module 3 › Hands-on: Draw Line › Code Walkthrough
Algorithm
  1. Compute base = 16384 + 128 * 32.
  2. Set D = 0xFFFF (all bits 1).
  3. Repeat 32 times: M = D; A = A + 1.
The loop writes full words so adjacent pixels join to form a continuous line.
Conceptual assembly outline
// compute base address for row 128
@16384
D = A
@128
D = D + A*32  // conceptual: compute 16384 + 128*32
@SCREEN_BASE
A = D
// set all bits
D = -1         // D = 0xFFFF
@COUNT
M = 32         // conceptual counter
(WRITE_LOOP)
M = D           // write 0xFFFF
@NEXT
A = A + 1       // advance to next word
...             // decrement counter and loop
Note: This outline is conceptual; the simulator uses standard Hack assembly instructions to implement arithmetic and looping.

screens.title: Set or clear a single pixel (read-modify-write)
screens.subtitle: Preserve neighbouring pixels by reading the word, changing a bit, and writing back

narration.text: To change a single pixel you must manipulate one bit inside a 16-bit word while keeping the other 15 bits unchanged. This read-modify-write pattern prevents accidentally erasing neighboring pixels that share the same word. The sequence is: compute the address and bit position, read the current 16-bit word from memory into D, construct a mask with a single 1 in the bit position, then either OR the mask to set the bit or AND the inverse of the mask to clear it. Finally, write the updated word back to memory. A concrete example: to set the pixel at row r, column c, compute address = 16384 + r*32 + c/16 and bit = c % 16. Read M into D, compute D = D | (1 << bit), then write M = D. A common beginner error is writing the mask directly to memory without first reading and merging: that replaces the whole word and destroys adjacent pixels. Practice building a small routine that takes row and column values and performs this read-modify-write safely. Set or clear a single pixel (read-modify-write) means always read the current word, modify only the target bit, and write the entire word back to avoid corrupting adjacent pixels.. In practical terms, preserve neighbouring pixels by reading the word, changing a bit, and writing back. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Read-modify-write is essential
keyIdea.text: Always read the current word, modify only the target bit, and write the entire word back to avoid corrupting adjacent pixels.

content.html:
Module 3 › Pixel Update › Process
Steps to change one pixel
  1. Compute wordIndex = row*32 + (col/16) and address = 16384 + wordIndex.
  2. Read M at that address into D.
  3. Create mask = 1 << (col % 16).
  4. Set: D = D | mask. Clear: D = D & ~mask.
  5. Write D back: M = D.
This preserves the other 15 bits controlled by the same memory word.
Analogy
Think of a word as a row of 16 light switches in a single box. To flip one switch you open the box, change the single switch, and close it again. Replacing the whole box would change all switches.
Common Mistake
Writing a mask directly to a screen address overwrites 15 neighboring pixels; always merge with the current word.

screens.title: Wait for a key and display its code
screens.subtitle: Poll address 24576, then draw or display the ASCII code

narration.text: A typical program listens for a key press by repeatedly reading the keyboard register at address 24576 until the returned value is non-zero. This polling loop is simple and effective for small programs. Once a non-zero ASCII value is read, the program can draw a visible representation on the screen by writing to one or more screen words using the pixel mapping routines you learned earlier. For example, a minimal program reads the keyboard register in a loop: if the value is zero continue looping; if non-zero, copy the ASCII code to a known memory location used by your display routine and call that routine to render a character. A subtlety is debouncing: if you want to avoid multiple detections for a single press, wait until the register reads zero again before resuming detection. Another common pattern is to display the numeric ASCII code: write a small number-to-text routine that draws digits on the screen. Practicing this pattern helps you combine memory reads, control flow, and the pixel-writing routines into a single user-facing feature. Wait for a key and display its code means read address 24576 in a loop; on non-zero value, act and optionally wait for it to return to zero to detect discrete presses.. In practical terms, poll address 24576, then draw or display the ascii code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Polling the keyboard
keyIdea.text: Read address 24576 in a loop; on non-zero value, act and optionally wait for it to return to zero to detect discrete presses.

content.html:
Module 3 › Keyboard Loop › Code Walkthrough
Polling pattern
// conceptual loop
(READ_KEY)
@24576
D = M         // D contains keyboard code or 0
@READ_KEY
D; JEQ         // if zero, jump back and keep polling
// D != 0: handle key
@DISPLAY_ADDR
M = D         // store code for display routine
// optionally wait for release
(WAIT_RELEASE)
@24576
D = M
@WAIT_RELEASE
D; JNE        // loop until keyboard returns 0
This outline shows the polling loop and a simple debounce that waits for the key to be released before continuing detection.
Display strategies
Display the raw ASCII as a number by converting digits and drawing them to the screen.
Or map printable ASCII to a bitmap font and draw the character pixels at a chosen screen location.
Key Takeaway
Polling is simple and works for small programs. For more complex input handling you would add buffering or interrupts, but those are beyond the Hack design used here.

screens.title: Assembling the complete Computer chip
screens.subtitle: CPU + Memory (including screen/keyboard) + ROM wired together

narration.text: The Computer chip brings together three components: the C P U, the Memory chip (which includes R A M, the screen memory range, and the keyboard register), and the ROM that holds the program. The PC output from the C P U wires to the ROM address input so instructions are fetched from ROM. The ROM output feeds the C P U's instruction input. The C P U produces outM, writeM, and addressM signals; these connect to the Memory chip, which responds by providing inM back to the C P U for load operations. The reset input initializes the C P U's program counter to zero so execution starts at the first ROM address. This composition is remarkably simple: no special input and output bus is present because input and output devices are part of the memory map. The HDL snippet from the chapter exactly captures this wiring. Conceptually, see three buildings: a ROM library where instructions live, a C P U factory that executes them, and a Memory warehouse that stores data and controls the screen and keyboard. Understanding this wiring helps you reason about where data flows when your program draws a pixel or reads the keyboard.

keyIdea.title: Three-part computer
keyIdea.text: Computer = ROM + CPU + Memory. Memory includes the screen and keyboard, so normal memory operations drive I/O.

content.html:
Module 3 › Computer Chip › Architecture
Components
  • ROM32K: instruction memory, addressed by PC.
  • CPU: executes instructions, outputs addressM, outM, writeM, and accepts inM.
  • Memory: RAM16K plus screen and keyboard memory-mapped ranges.
Reset initializes the PC so the ROM fetch begins at the program's start address.
HDL snippet
CHIP Computer {
    IN reset;

    PARTS:
    ROM32K(address=pc, out=instruction);
    CPU(inM=inM, instruction=instruction, reset=reset, outM=outM, writeM=writeM, addressM=addressM, pc=pc);
    Memory(in=outM, load=writeM, address=addressM, out=inM);
}
This HDL shows the direct wiring: the CPU drives the Memory using the same address and write signals used for ordinary RAM operations, which makes the screen and keyboard accessible through the same path.

screens.title: Memory layout and capacities
screens.subtitle: How much space the screen uses and what remains for data

narration.text: The Hack data memory provides 16K words in total. The screen occupies addresses 16384 through 24575, which is 8,192 words. The keyboard sits at 24576 as a single register. That means exactly half of the data memory addresses are reserved for the screen, leaving the other half for program data. The screen's 8,192 words control 131,072 pixels, so the ratio is one word per 16 pixels. This compact representation is efficient in memory usage but requires bit-level manipulation when changing individual pixels. screens.subtitle: Why the Hack chooses memory-mapped I/O and what you give up

narration.text: Memory-mapped input and output offers clear benefits: simplicity, uniformity, and flexibility. The C P U needs no special opcodes, so the same load and store instructions drive devices and memory. Addressing and addressing modes are unified, and adding a new device is a matter of reserving address space rather than extending the instruction set. However, there are trade-offs. Software must perform address arithmetic and often bit manipulation to control devices, which can be more complex than high-level, built-in device instructions. Performance can be comparable for many tasks but specialized input and output instructions or dedicated buses can be more efficient for high-throughput devices. For the educational Hack computer the choice emphasizes clarity and minimal hardware, making it easier to understand how software maps to hardware.
